_scope_definitions.all: Every paper in the module (all are causal / potential-outcomes analyses of treatment effects). Fires unconditionally.
_scope_definitions.observational: The paper states that its treatment-effect estimates come from non-randomized data and relies on a selection-on-observables / unconfoundedness identifying assumption. Does NOT fire for: a randomized experiment (even one that also runs adjusted regressions), or a design whose identification the paper attributes to randomization or an instrument.
_scope_definitions.iv: The paper states it identifies effects through an instrumental variable, or a fuzzy regression-discontinuity estimated by two-stage least squares. Does NOT fire when: the paper merely calls a policy an 'instrument' informally with no IV identification claim; a variable is used only as a control; standard errors happen to be clustered.
_scope_definitions.generalization: The paper states it carries an estimate from its study sample to a different or broader target population (population effect, transportability, external target). Does NOT fire for: a passing remark about external validity; reporting subgroup effects that stay within the study sample.
_scope_definitions.interaction_model: The paper states it estimates a multiplicative interaction / product term (treatment x moderator, or X x Z) to test a conditional or moderating hypothesis. Does NOT fire for: adding a covariate as a control with no product term; reporting means by subgroup with no product term; a stratified analysis with no interaction coefficient.
_scope_definitions.nonlinear_interaction: interaction_model AND the outcome model is a nonlinear / limited-dependent model the paper names (logit, probit, tobit, Poisson or other count, duration/hazard, ordered, multinomial). Does NOT fire for: a linear/OLS interaction; a nonlinear model that contains no product or higher-order term.
_scope_definitions.multiple_hypotheses: The paper states it tests a family of several hypotheses at once -- treatment effects on multiple outcomes, or across multiple subgroups/treatments -- and reports the tests together. Does NOT fire for: a single pre-specified primary outcome/hypothesis; incidental coefficients from one model that the paper does not treat as a tested family.
_scope_definitions.heterogeneity_test: Fires when the paper states it performs a statistical test for the presence of effect variation (an omnibus or constant-effect test, a variance-ratio test, a shifted-CDF/KS test, or a randomization test of no heterogeneity). Near-miss that does NOT fire: comparing two subgroup point estimates with no test; a test of the overall average effect.
_scope_definitions.causal_forest: The paper states it uses a random / causal / regression forest to estimate treatment effects and to build confidence intervals. Does NOT fire for: a single descriptive regression tree; a random-effects (multilevel) model; a forest used only for propensity or nuisance prediction that the paper does not use for effect inference.
_scope_definitions.quantile_distributional: The paper states a quantile treatment effect or a distributional / CDF treatment effect as an estimand it reports. Does NOT fire for: reporting subgroup means; a single median regression the paper does not frame as a distributional-effect claim.
_scope_definitions.clustered: The paper states its observations are clustered or otherwise dependent (e.g., pupils within classrooms, siblings, repeated measures on a unit) and describes that grouping. Does NOT fire for: a single cross-section the paper treats as independent units; time fixed effects alone.
_scope_definitions.subgroup_analysis: Fires when the paper states it reports or tests treatment effects for subgroups defined by covariates. Near-miss that does NOT fire: reporting only the overall average effect; adjusting for a covariate without any subgroup-specific effect.
_scope_definitions.data_driven_hte: Fires when the paper states it uses a data-adaptive/machine-learning method to discover or estimate heterogeneity (causal forest, penalized/LASSO selection, ensemble/super-learner, causal or recursive-partitioning trees, BART). Near-miss that does NOT fire: pre-registered fixed subgroups fit by OLS.
_scope_definitions.linear_interaction: interaction_model estimated by a linear (OLS-type) specification in which at least one interacted variable is continuous. Does NOT fire for: a fully saturated dummy-by-dummy model with no continuous interacted variable; a nonlinear-link model.
_scope_definitions.subgroup_heterogeneity: The paper states that variation of the treatment effect across subpopulations (heterogeneous / conditional / effect-modified effects) is a quantity it targets and reports. Does NOT fire for: a single robustness split the paper does not frame as a heterogeneity estimand; reporting only an overall average effect.
_scope_definitions.risk_modeling: The paper states it stratifies or predicts treatment effects using a baseline-risk / prognostic model or risk score. Does NOT fire for: one-variable-at-a-time subgroup analysis; adjusting for baseline covariates without forming a risk score.
_scope_definitions.trimming: The paper states it discards or trims units by their estimated propensity score, or restricts the analysis to a common-support / overlap region. Does NOT fire for: dropping units for item-missing data; winsorizing or trimming the outcome variable.
_scope_definitions.attrition: The paper states it has non-trivial follow-up attrition or missing outcome data. Does NOT fire for: complete outcome data; missingness confined to covariates.

flag_condition: The paper reports treatment-effect estimates with no statement of a no-interference / SUTVA assumption and no treatment of possible spillover between units.
severity_basis: Athey (2021) and Bargagli (2022) treat no-interference/SUTVA as a maintained condition for the effects to be defined; Imai (2010) requires re-leveling the analysis when interference is present.
requirement_statement: The paper should state the no-interference / SUTVA assumption its effect estimates rely on, or show how the design rules interference out.

claim: In a nonlinear / limited-dependent model the interaction effect is the cross-partial derivative (or cross-difference) of the predicted outcome, not the coefficient on the product term; the coefficient can be zero while the effect is nonzero, its sign can differ from the effect's, and the effect varies across observations -- so magnitude must be computed from the cross-partial, and tools that return a single coefficient-based marginal effect for an interacted variable give the wrong answer.
observable: How the paper obtains the interaction effect's magnitude: from the estimated cross-partial derivative/difference of predicted outcomes, or by reading the product-term coefficient.
pass_condition: The paper computes the interaction effect as a cross-partial derivative or discrete cross-difference of the predicted outcome (or as marginal effects on the predicted scale), at stated covariate values or averaged over units.
flag_condition: The paper reports the product-term coefficient (its size or sign) as the interaction effect in a nonlinear model, or reads the effect off a single tool-generated marginal effect for the interacted variable.
severity_basis: Ai (2003) and Norton (2004) show the interaction effect must be computed as the cross derivative and can be nonzero when the coefficient is zero; Mize (2019) calls the product-term coefficient a misleading representation.
requirement_statement: A nonlinear-model interaction effect should be computed from the cross-partial of the predicted outcome, not the product-term coefficient.

claim: When a family of hypotheses, outcomes, or subgroups is tested at once, the chance of at least one false rejection far exceeds the nominal level, so inference must account for multiplicity -- through a correction (Bonferroni/Holm, resampling-based FWER, or an FDR procedure), a summary index, or by reporting adjusted alongside unadjusted results -- rather than emphasizing whichever tests happened to reach significance.
observable: Whether the paper adjusts inference for the number of tests in the family, or reports a summary index, versus reporting only per-test unadjusted significance.
pass_condition: For the tested family the paper reports a named multiplicity adjustment (Bonferroni, Holm, FWER resampling, Benjamini-Hochberg/FDR) or a summary index, or presents adjusted results alongside unadjusted ones.
flag_condition: The paper reports only per-test unadjusted p-values / significance for a family of hypotheses or outcomes and highlights the significant subset with no multiplicity adjustment.
severity_basis: List (2019) and Anderson (2008) state that with many tests some are significant by chance and inference must account for multiplicity; Anderson (2008) calls emphasizing the unadjusted significant subset unreliable.
prevalence_aggravator: Anderson (2008) reports most surveyed randomized evaluations tested five or more outcomes, so unadjusted multiple testing is widespread.
requirement_statement: A paper testing a family of hypotheses/outcomes should report multiplicity-adjusted inference or a summary index.

observable: Whether the paper's variation test aligns for the average effect and handles the unknown ATE nuisance validly (e.g., a randomization test maximized over an ATE confidence interval), versus a naive distributional test compared to an unadjusted null.
pass_condition: The paper's heterogeneity test aligns for the mean effect and uses a null that accounts for the estimated-ATE nuisance (e.g., FRT over an ATE confidence interval).
flag_condition: The paper tests for heterogeneity with a naive distributional statistic (e.g., a plain or plug-in shifted Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) compared to the ordinary null distribution.
severity_basis: Plugging the estimated ATE into the ordinary null yields invalid p-values (Ding 2015).
requirement_statement: A test for effect variation must isolate variation from the mean shift and validly handle the unknown-ATE nuisance.

claim: Scanning the conditional marginal effect across values of a moderator is itself a multiple-comparison problem: standard pointwise intervals are miscalibrated for the intended test, so reporting any single significant marginal effect across the moderator produces excess false positives, and joint tests of pre-specified predictions need a corrected (e.g., bootstrap-derived) critical value.
observable: Whether the paper corrects for the many implied comparisons when reporting marginal-effect significance across a moderator, or reports whichever value of the moderator yielded significance using pointwise intervals.
pass_condition: The paper reports marginal-effect significance across the moderator using a multiplicity- or joint-test-corrected procedure (FWER/FDR control or a bootstrap critical value), or tests pre-specified predictions jointly.
flag_condition: The paper reports a significant conditional marginal effect found by scanning values of the moderator with uncorrected pointwise intervals.
severity_basis: Esarey (2017) shows an interaction implicitly splits the sample by the moderator, making pointwise intervals too wide or too narrow and any-value reporting overconfident.
requirement_statement: Marginal-effect significance scanned across a moderator should be corrected for the implied multiple comparisons.

claim: Subgroups or heterogeneity variables chosen after seeing the outcomes produce spurious findings, so heterogeneity claims must rest on pre-specified subgroups or on a discovery/inference separation (sample splitting, a held-out test set, or cross-validated tuning).
observable: Whether the reported heterogeneity was pre-specified or protected by a discovery-versus-inference data split.
pass_condition: The paper states the subgroups / heterogeneity variables were specified before analysis, OR that discovery and final inference use separate data (sample splitting, a held-out test set, or cross-validation for model/tuning selection).
flag_condition: The paper reports subgroup or data-driven heterogeneity formed after examining outcomes with no pre-specification and no discovery/inference split.
severity_basis: Imai (2010) and Wager (2018) tie post-hoc subgrouping to spurious significant findings and require subgroups be fixed in advance or validated out of sample.
requirement_statement: Heterogeneity claims must be pre-specified or protected by a discovery/inference data split.

claim: A linear multiplicative interaction assumes the marginal effect changes at a constant (linear) rate with the moderator; if this fails, the conditional-effect estimates are biased and inconsistent, so the paper should assess the assumption -- via a diagnostic plot or a more flexible (binning/kernel) estimator that nests the linear model -- and where linearity is doubtful prefer the flexible estimate.
observable: Whether the paper assesses the constant-marginal-effect (linearity) assumption of its linear interaction, e.g. through a diagnostic plot or a binning/flexible estimator, rather than assuming it.
pass_condition: The paper reports a check of the linear-interaction assumption (diagnostic plot, or a binning/kernel/flexible estimate compared against the linear model) and interprets effects consistent with the result.
flag_condition: The paper reports conditional effects at moderator values from a linear interaction with no assessment of the constant-marginal-effect assumption.
severity_basis: Hainmueller (2018) shows that when the linear-interaction assumption fails the conditional-effect estimates are inconsistent and biased, and that a binning estimator that diverges from the linear model signals invalidity.

claim: Conditional or subgroup effects should be reported only over regions of the moderator/covariate space with enough data (and treatment variation); where a region is sparse the estimate rests on extrapolation and model form rather than observations, so it is fragile and should not be presented as an evidenced effect.
observable: Whether the paper reports conditional/subgroup effects only where data are adequate, or extends them into sparse regions without flagging the reliance on extrapolation.
pass_condition: The paper limits reported conditional effects to regions with adequate data density (or marks sparse-region estimates as extrapolation, e.g., via a moderator histogram or observation counts).
flag_condition: The paper reports conditional/subgroup effects in sparse regions of the moderator/covariate space without noting the reliance on extrapolation or the thinness of the data.
severity_basis: Hainmueller (2018) states effect estimates where data are sparse are fragile and model-dependent; Grimmer (2017) notes naive subgroup differences in sparse cells reflect chance rather than systematic effects.
requirement_statement: Conditional effects should be reported only where the data are adequate, and sparse-region estimates marked as extrapolation.

claim: A risk-based (predictive) heterogeneity analysis rests on the dependence of the absolute effect on baseline risk; the stratifying risk model must be developed blinded to treatment assignment (fit without a treatment-assignment term), and an internally developed model must use the whole trial population rather than the control arm alone, which otherwise induces or exaggerates treatment-by-risk interactions.
observable: Whether the paper states its risk/prognostic model was fit without a treatment-assignment term and, if internal, on the full trial population rather than controls only.
pass_condition: The paper states the risk model was developed blinded to treatment (no treatment-assignment term) and, if internally developed, on the entire trial population.
flag_condition: The paper stratifies by a risk model without stating it was blinded to treatment, or reports an internal model fit on the control arm only.
severity_basis: Kent (2019) defines risk modeling by a subgrouping scheme blinded to treatment, requires fitting without a treatment term, and warns that control-only fitting exaggerates treatment-by-risk interactions.
requirement_statement: A stratifying risk model should be fit blinded to treatment and (if internal) on the whole trial population.

claim: A subsample-selection or trimming rule for handling limited overlap must be defined from the joint distribution of covariates and treatment (e.g., the propensity score) alone and must not use the outcomes, because a selection rule that depends on the outcome distribution introduces deliberate bias into the estimated effects.
observable: Whether the paper's trimming / subsample-selection rule is defined from covariates/propensity only, or in a way that uses outcome data.
pass_condition: The paper defines its trimming/overlap-selection rule from covariates and treatment (e.g., propensity-score bounds) without reference to outcomes.
flag_condition: The paper defines its trimming/selection rule using the outcome distribution (e.g., dropping units by their outcomes or outcome variances).
severity_basis: Crump (2009) requires the subsample-selection rule to depend only on covariates and treatment so as not to introduce deliberate bias with respect to the outcomes.
requirement_statement: A trimming/overlap-selection rule should be based on covariates/propensity, not on outcomes.

claim: Because the interaction effect in a nonlinear model varies in sign and magnitude across observations, a single summary number is inadequate; the paper should convey the effect's distribution -- reporting predicted outcomes/probabilities for the focal variables, and where a focal variable is continuous a visualization of the effect across its values.
observable: Whether the paper reports predicted values/probabilities or the distribution of the interaction effect across observations, rather than only one summary number.
pass_condition: The paper reports predicted outcomes/probabilities for the interacting variables, or the distribution of the interaction effect across covariate values (a plot where a focal variable is continuous).
flag_condition: The paper conveys a nonlinear interaction only through a single summary number or the product-term coefficient, with no predicted values/distribution reported.
severity_basis: Mize (2019) states reporting the predictions/predicted probabilities is necessary to convey the substantive interaction; Ai (2003) notes a single summary measure is inadequate because the effect differs across observations.
requirement_statement: A nonlinear interaction should be reported as predicted values / an effect distribution, not one summary number.

claim: Heterogeneity is scale-dependent: whether an effect is constant or varies depends on the outcome scale (e.g., absolute risk difference vs. relative effect), and a constant relative effect generally implies a varying absolute effect. A paper claiming or denying heterogeneity must therefore state the scale on which it is measured.
observable: Whether the paper states the outcome scale (absolute vs. relative, or a named transformation) on which it assesses effect heterogeneity/constancy.
pass_condition: The paper states the scale on which heterogeneity is measured (e.g., absolute difference, ratio, or a named transformation), or reports the effect on more than one scale.
flag_condition: The paper claims or denies heterogeneity without stating the outcome scale it is measured on.
severity_basis: Kent (2019) calls heterogeneity a scale-dependent concept and notes the absolute difference varies even when the relative effect is constant; Ding (2015) states constancy depends critically on the outcome scale.
requirement_statement: A paper asserting or denying heterogeneity should state the outcome scale it is measured on.

claim: When follow-up attrition or missing outcomes may differ by treatment status, they can bias treatment-control comparisons; the paper should assess this -- e.g., by imputing missing outcomes and examining worst-case bounds, or re-estimating after handling the attrition -- rather than analyzing complete cases without comment.
observable: Whether the paper, given non-trivial attrition/missing outcomes, assesses the sensitivity of its results (imputation, bounds, or re-estimation) rather than reporting complete cases only.
pass_condition: The paper reports an assessment of attrition/missing-outcome sensitivity (imputation, worst-case bounds, or a re-estimation) or evidence attrition is unrelated to treatment.
flag_condition: The paper reports non-trivial attrition/missing outcomes but analyzes complete cases with no sensitivity assessment.
severity_basis: Anderson (2008) states attrition related to treatment can create systematic differences unrelated to the treatment and calls for imputation and worst-case analysis; Ding (2015) notes complete-case restriction can create inferential problems.
requirement_statement: A paper with non-trivial attrition should assess its sensitivity rather than silently analyze complete cases.
